summary.text: Introduce the auxiliary recurrences \(u_{n+2}=-4u_{n+1}-64u_n\) and \(y_{n+2}=-4y_{n+1}-64y_n\), and show from matching initial values and the fourth-order recurrence that \(a_n=2\cdot8^n-2(-8)^n+y_n\). A preserved quadratic invariant for \(u\) yields \(y_{2n+1}=u_{n+1}^2-32\cdot64^n\), while the two exponential terms contribute \(32\cdot64^n\) at odd indices, so they cancel and give \(a_{2n+1}=u_{n+1}^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term is a square in \(\mathbb Z\).

Introduce two auxiliary integer sequences \((u_n)\) and \((y_n)\) by
\[
u_0=1,\qquad u_1=-2,\qquad
u_{n+2}=-4u_{n+1}-64u_n,
\]
and
\[
y_0=-1,\qquad y_1=-28,\qquad
y_{n+2}=-4y_{n+1}-64y_n.
\]
We will ultimately prove the explicit square identity
\[
 a_{2n+1}=u_{n+1}^2.
\]

First we connect \(a\) to the simpler second-order sequence \(y\). The recurrence for \(y\), applied twice, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{n+4}
  &=-4y_{n+3}-64y_{n+2}\\
  &=-4y_{n+3}-64(-4y_{n+1}-64y_n)\\
  &=-4y_{n+3}+256y_{n+1}+4096y_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(y\) also obeys the fourth-order recurrence defining \(a\).

Define
\[
b_n=2\cdot 8^n-2\cdot(-8)^n+y_n.
\]
The geometric sequences \(8^n\) and \((-8)^n\) obey the same fourth-order recurrence. Indeed, for \(r=8\) and for \(r=-8\), one has
\[
r^4=-4r^3+256r+4096.
\]
Multiplying this identity by \(r^n\) gives
\[
r^{n+4}=-4r^{n+3}+256r^{n+1}+4096r^n.
\]
Together with the fourth-order recurrence just established for \(y\), this shows that
\[
b_{n+4}=-4b_{n+3}+256b_{n+1}+4096b_n.
\]

We now compare the initial values of \(a\) and \(b\). From the recurrence for \(y\),
\[
y_2=-4(-28)-64(-1)=176
\]
and
\[
y_3=-4(176)-64(-28)=1088.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_0&=2-2-1=-1,\\
b_1&=2\cdot8-2\cdot(-8)-28=4,\\
b_2&=2\cdot64-2\cdot64+176=176,\\
b_3&=2\cdot512-2\cdot(-512)+1088=3136.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a_j=b_j\) for \(j=0,1,2,3\). Since the two sequences obey the same recurrence, it follows by strong induction that
\[
a_n=b_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\]
Explicitly, after the four base cases, if this equality is known at all earlier indices and the current index is \(n+4\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+4}
 &=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n\\
 &=-4b_{n+3}+256b_{n+1}+4096b_n\\
 &=b_{n+4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice that the recurrence has coefficient zero at the \(n+2\) term, so precisely the three indicated earlier values are needed.

The next ingredient is a quadratic invariant for \(u\): for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
 u_{n+1}^2+4u_nu_{n+1}+64u_n^2=60\cdot64^n. \tag{1}
\]
For \(n=0\), its left side is
\[
(-2)^2+4(1)(-2)+64(1)^2=4-8+64=60,
\]
which is the right side. Suppose (1) holds at \(n\). Using
\(u_{n+2}=-4u_{n+1}-64u_n\), direct expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&u_{n+2}^2+4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}+64u_{n+1}^2\\
&\quad=(-4u_{n+1}-64u_n)^2
 +4u_{n+1}(-4u_{n+1}-64u_n)+64u_{n+1}^2\\
&\quad=64\bigl(u_{n+1}^2+4u_nu_{n+1}+64u_n^2\bigr)\\
&\quad=64(60\cdot64^n)=60\cdot64^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1) by induction.

We next prove, simultaneously, formulas for the even and odd terms of \(y\):
\[
\boxed{\ y_{2n}=u_nu_{n+1}+64^n\ }, \tag{2}
\]
\[
\boxed{\ y_{2n+1}=u_{n+1}^2-32\cdot64^n\ }. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=0\), the right side of (2) is
\(u_0u_1+1=(1)(-2)+1=-1=y_0\), while the right side of (3) is
\(u_1^2-32=4-32=-28=y_1\).

Assume (2) and (3) hold for a fixed \(n\). First, the recurrence for \(y\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{2n+2}
 &=-4y_{2n+1}-64y_{2n}\\
 &=-4\bigl(u_{n+1}^2-32\cdot64^n\bigr)
   -64\bigl(u_nu_{n+1}+64^n\bigr)\\
 &=u_{n+1}(-4u_{n+1}-64u_n)+64\cdot64^n\\
 &=u_{n+1}u_{n+2}+64^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is formula (2) with \(n+1\) in place of \(n\).

For the next odd term, use this newly proved even formula together with the inductive odd formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{2n+3}
 &=-4y_{2n+2}-64y_{2n+1}\\
 &=-4\bigl(u_{n+1}u_{n+2}+64^{n+1}\bigr)
   -64\bigl(u_{n+1}^2-32\cdot64^n\bigr)\\
 &=-4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}-64u_{n+1}^2+28\cdot64^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the last step, the scalar terms combine because
\(-4\cdot64^{n+1}+32\cdot64^{n+1}=28\cdot64^{n+1}\).
Now split \(28=60-32\) and apply invariant (1) at index \(n+1\):
\[
60\cdot64^{n+1}
=u_{n+2}^2+4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}+64u_{n+1}^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{2n+3}
&=-4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}-64u_{n+1}^2
  +60\cdot64^{n+1}-32\cdot64^{n+1}\\
&=-4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}-64u_{n+1}^2\\
&\qquad{}+ igl(u_{n+2}^2+4u_{n+1}u_{n+2}
                   +64u_{n+1}^2\bigr)-32\cdot64^{n+1}\\
&=u_{n+2}^2-32\cdot64^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is formula (3) at \(n+1\), completing the simultaneous induction.

It remains to examine the geometric part of \(b_{2n+1}\). For every \(n\ge0\),
\[
2\cdot8^{2n+1}-2\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}=32\cdot64^n. \tag{4}
\]
One can see this immediately from
\(8^{2n+1}=8\cdot64^n\) and
\((-8)^{2n+1}=-8\cdot64^n\). Equivalently, (4) follows by induction: its value at \(n=0\) is \(16-2(-8)=32\), and increasing \(n\) by one multiplies both powers on the left by \(8^2=(-8)^2=64\), hence multiplies the entire difference by \(64\), exactly as on the right.

Finally, fix any nonnegative integer \(n\). Since \(a=b\), formula (4), followed by the odd-index formula (3), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}
 &=b_{2n+1}\\
 &=2\cdot8^{2n+1}-2\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}+y_{2n+1}\\
 &=32\cdot64^n+\bigl(u_{n+1}^2-32\cdot64^n\bigr)\\
 &=u_{n+1}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a_{2n+1}\) is the square of the integer \(u_{n+1}\) for every \(n\ge0\), proving the conjecture.
